content: Umbilical venous catheters (UVCs) are frequently utilized in the neonatal period to provide vascular access. A UVC is inserted through the umbilicus and follows a specific anatomical path: it traverses the umbilical vein, the left portal vein, the ductus venosus, the middle or left hepatic vein, and the inferior vena cava (IVC) before reaching the junction of the IVC and the right atrium. In contrast, the paired umbilical arteries initially course caudally to enter the right and left iliac arteries. This anatomical distinction allows for easy differentiation between the umbilical venous catheter and the umbilical artery catheter on abdominal radiographs. The UVC predominantly follows an anterior and cephalad trajectory in the midline umbilical vein until it is directed posteriorly within the liver. Conversely, the umbilical artery catheter initially courses caudally and posteriorly to enter either the right or left iliac artery before ascending superiorly within the more posteriorly positioned aorta. The optimal placement of the UVC tip is typically in the cephalad portion of the inferior vena cava or at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium. Anomalous positioning of the Umbilical Venous Catheter Anomalous positioning of the UVC is a common occurrence, often due to its insertion by pediatricians without imaging guidance. If the UVC follows the normal course to the inferior vena cava or right atrium but is advanced too far, it may extend through a patent foramen ovale or an atrial septal defect into the left atrium. If advanced further, it could enter a pulmonary vein. Alternatively, the catheter may continue through the right atrium into the superior vena cava or cross the tricuspid valve to enter the right ventricle. If advanced even further, the UVC may extend into the main, right, or left pulmonary artery. If the UVC reaches the left portal vein but does not continue into the ductus venosus, it may deviate leftward into the more peripheral left portal vein or rightward, where it could eventually course into the right portal vein or hepatofugally into the main portal vein. In some cases, it may extend further into the vessels that converge to form the portal vein, such as the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. Complications of the Umbilical Venous Catheter If the UVC perforates an intrahepatic vascular wall, it may result in the formation of a hepatic hematoma. Intravascular thrombi can develop along the course of the UVC. The UVC may also perforate the right or left atrial wall, potentially entering the pericardial space.
